system_instruction:
You write a short evidence brief on the lung cancer care pathway for one Finnish wellbeing services county, for the county's health managers. You may use ONLY the claims provided. Each claim has an ID, a status and a text.

Rules:
1. Every sentence must list the IDs of the claims it relies on in claim_ids (at least one). Use IDs exactly as given. Do not cite anything that is not in the list.
2. Copy every number exactly as it appears in a cited claim, at the same precision. Do NOT calculate new numbers (no differences, ratios or percentage-point gaps): state the county value and the national value side by side instead. Spell out no numbers in words.
3. State uncertainty. Give 95% confidence intervals where the claim has one. Never say "certain": say the 95% confidence interval excludes (or includes) the national value. Say that the county shares are crude (not adjusted for age or stage). Where an age-adjusted value exists (Kuva 16, digitised from a figure, about ±0.5 percentage points), use it to say whether a gap holds after age adjustment, say it is digitised, and pass on any caveat in the claim's notes (e.g. a confidence interval that could not be read).
4. The treatment categories overlap (a patient can have several); never add them up or present them as a breakdown. "No treatment record within 12 months" mixes untreated patients and treatment that was not recorded; never call it "untreated" or "missing data". MDT records measure recording practice, not care.
5. Read the no-treatment-record share as a data-quality signal, and present that reading as an inference, not a finding. If it is at or below the national value, this is consistent with relatively complete treatment recording (it is not direct evidence of it), so a low curative share is less likely to be only a recording artefact; do not cite a low no-record share as a reason to fix recording. If it is above national, a low share of a treatment type may partly reflect unrecorded treatment.
6. Label status in the sentence itself: a sentence citing a claim with status "preliminary" must say "preliminary" (e.g. "preliminary, unpublished figures"); one citing "mentor insight" must say "mentor insight". Claims "verified by Hellu" were read in full by a teammate in documents we do not hold locally (regional pathway documents, the Health Care Act, THL guidance, a journal article); describe them by what they are, not as regional documents unless they are. Every sentence that cites a county share (a claim whose ID starts with "cty:") must say the share is crude (the word "crude"). A sentence citing a claim with status "recommendation (ours)" must say it is the team's recommendation (e.g. "the team recommends"). In what_to_do_first, cite the relevant team recommendation (rec:1, rec:2 or rec:3) together with the evidence claims that support it; do not add steps that are in neither.
7. Respect each claim's scope ("scope: …" in its notes). Never use a claim for something outside its scope: e.g. the HILMO ~90% claim concerns diagnosis concordance only and says nothing about treatment recording; a regional finding describes only the named region's document; national averages are not county figures.
8. Describe planned national measures as plans, with the plan's own verb and date, in the present tense: e.g. "the roadmap plans national pathways with target access times for five cancers by 2026–2028"; "the Filha programme's diagnostics recommendation is due to be completed before the 2030 mid-term evaluation". A recommendation being completed is not the same as it being implemented. Never write "will" about national measures. Never use the words certain, proves, guarantees or definitely.
9. Each section has a headline (the main point, one sentence of at most 30 words, with claim IDs) and 2–4 detail sentences. "where_we_lag": where this county's pathway lags national values. "how_sure_are_we": what is well supported, what is uncertain and what public data cannot show. "what_to_do_first": the first steps, drawn from the team's draft recommendations and suited to this county's data, each backed by evidence claims.
10. Plain, direct English. No claims about other counties. No headings or numbering inside sentences. Apply these rules and the claim notes by writing accurately; do not restate them in the brief (do not write things like "completing is not the same as implementing" or "this describes only its own document"), and keep each sentence under about 60 words.

headline.text: Pohjois-Pohjanmaa lags the national share in crude curative treatment at 23.6% versus 27.0% nationally and in crude recorded multidisciplinary team meetings at 1.1% versus 6.0%.

details.text: Among 1050 new lung cancer patients in 2019–2023, the county's crude curative treatment share was 23.6% (95% CI 21.1–26.3; n=248/1050), where the 95% confidence interval excludes the national value of 27.0% (4009/14873), and these crude shares are not adjusted for age or stage.

In overlapping treatment categories where patients can receive multiple types, the crude life-prolonging share was 37.4% (95% CI 34.5–40.4; n=393/1050), with its 95% confidence interval excluding the national 30.4% (4522/14873), while the crude symptomatic share of 38.8% (95% CI 35.9–41.7; n=407/1050) has a 95% confidence interval that includes the national 39.5% (5871/14873).

The crude share of patients with a multidisciplinary team meeting recorded in HILMO was 1.1% (95% CI 0.7–2.0; n=12/1050), whose 95% confidence interval excludes the national 6.0% (893/14873), and this measures recording practice from direct patient contacts rather than actual multidisciplinary review.

headline.text: The low crude curative share is unlikely to be only a recording artefact, but crude figures lack stage adjustment and public data omit key pathway timestamps.

details.text: The crude share with no treatment record within 12 months—mixing untreated patients and unrecorded treatment—is 25.0% (95% CI 22.5–27.8; n=263/1050), with its 95% confidence interval including the national 27.5% (4089/14873); as an inference, not a finding, this is consistent with relatively complete recording (not direct evidence), making the 23.6% crude curative share less likely to be only a recording artefact.

Although a figure digitised at ±0.5 percentage points shows national age-adjusted curative shares of 26.7% for men and 26.9% for women, county shares here are crude, stage is missing for nearly half of new patients nationally, and a journal article's roughly 90% HILMO–Cancer Registry match covers diagnosis concordance only, not treatment or multidisciplinary recording.

While preliminary, unpublished national averages show 155 days from symptoms to treatment in Finland (56 days patient delay, 41 days primary care, 58 days specialist care), outpatient primary care visits and occupational health are not included in the report's data, which also lack timestamps for symptoms, referrals, imaging, first specialist visits, and treatment start.

headline.text: To address the lower crude curative share of 23.6%, the team recommends tracking THL 21/2016 access times, standardising referrals and diagnostic contacts, and auditing stage and multidisciplinary coding completeness.

details.text: Because the Health Care Act §52 sets no legal maximum time for a cancer suspicion and national target access times are only planned for 2026–2028 (with Filha's diagnostics guideline due before the 2030 interim evaluation), the team recommends reporting referral-to-treatment access times using THL Ohjaus 21/2016 definitions for 16 cancers and flagging stalled handovers.

Since patients are referred under local instructions, a mentor insight notes weak referrals receive lower specialist urgency ratings, and national referral criteria and care-coordinator guidance are only planned for 2026–2028 (for county adoption in 2029–2031), the team recommends a standard referral template, referring persistent symptoms after a normal X-ray to a pulmonologist, and naming a diagnostic-phase contact.

Given the county's 1.1% crude recorded multidisciplinary meeting share versus 6.0% nationally, missing stage data for nearly half of new patients nationally, and incomplete national reporting while a quality registry with 90% coverage is planned, the team recommends publishing county recording completeness for stage, drug treatment, and multidisciplinary coding and reading gaps as data-quality signals first.
